Experiments — capacity-constrained policy learning
Experiments report · end-to-end capacity-constrained policy learning

Fresh experiments across three datasets, plus a τ-feasibility study

Multi-seed N-sweeps on Criteo Uplift (real, 14M-row source), LaLonde NSW+PSID-1 (real) and the non-nested synthetic DGP; the full snapshot method comparison; and a new temperature study that measures the F-vs-G capacity asymmetry. All run on the refactored pipeline after closing the last verification gap. Charts are interactive: hover for exact values, click the method chips to add/remove series (axes rescale to what's visible).

Suggested items · done

Verification gap closed, LaLonde regenerated, loader repaired

The three follow-ups from the cleanup report are done. (1) The Criteo path — the one pipeline never executed end-to-end — required an unplanned fix first: the scikit-uplift S3 bucket both loaders pointed at now returns 403 Forbidden, so data_criteo.py gained a source-fallback chain (official Hugging Face mirror of criteo-research-uplift-v2.1, ~14M rows) and a deterministic local derivation for the discontinued 10% file. With data in hand, one full Criteo cell was run twice — once on the pre-refactor code (git worktree of HEAD), once on the refactored pipeline — with identical seeds: all 220 numeric outputs match to 0.0, completing the old-vs-new equivalence proof on all three dataset families. (2) results/lalonde_sweep.csv was regenerated under the fixed deterministic IPW seed. (3) Folding train_policies onto cell_core was considered and deliberately skipped: those two single-process harnesses train once and simulate many seeds — a genuinely different flow, and collapsing it would have changed the reproduction path of the paper's figures for no dedup gain.

The seed bug is worth seeing directly. Deriving the same three IPW seeds in three separate Python processes, old code versus new:

processold — hash((method,"ipw"))new — zlib.crc32
11616567850, 957704402, 39342621734278652634, 2518689814,
4006701070 (identical)
22706410794, 1897093115, 4281397572
33555958854, 3308010319, 3682734609

Python salts string hashes per process, so the random policy's reported IPW value on LaLonde changed on every run — silently, because the deterministic methods were unaffected and nothing ever errored.

For the paper

The two publication figures

Corrections · previously flagged, now fixed

Four issues that were documented but not repaired

The cleanup report listed five issues as “flagged, deliberately not changed.” Four of them affect numbers a referee would ask about, so they are now fixed and every real-data result on this page was regenerated afterwards. The fifth (a legacy script that swept a single data realization) was already retired.

IssueWhy it matteredFix
Propensity & scaler leak
data_criteo, data_lalonde		 Both were fit on the pooled data before the train/eval split, so eval rows informed the IPW weights that the same eval split was then scored with. This inflates held-out IPW for every method at once — the kind of thing that survives review until someone checks. Split first; fit both on train only and apply to eval. Verified: train features now standardize to exactly zero mean, eval to 0.00051 — eval is genuinely held out.
Survivorship bias
mean_oracle_outcome_served		 Averaging over served arrivals only rewards a policy for abandoning hard cases. Measured on treat-all against a 10% cap: 1.43 served-only versus 0.33 population, with 83% never served — a 4× overstatement. Added mean_oracle_outcome_all, which charges unserved arrivals their control-arm outcome. Both are reported; the population one is the comparable quantity.
Deployment mismatch
real_queue_experiment		 It sampled the softmax policy with no capacity buffer while every sweep deployed argmax after re-pricing at 0.92·b — so two numbers labelled “F” were not comparable. --deployment {argmax,softmax}, defaulting to argmax to match the sweeps. The old behaviour stays reachable and is documented as non-comparable.
Eval-μ peek
legacy/run_cell		 The *-mu variants re-solve μ on the eval split. The project reverted this convention in commit 3efaf40, but the variants were still produced by default. Off by default; reachable only via an explicit --with-eval-mu opt-in.

Only the first of these changes the paper's numbers materially, and it changes them in the conservative direction — held-out IPW values on Criteo and LaLonde are now estimated with weights that never saw the evaluation rows. Every real-data figure and table on this page was regenerated from scratch after the fix; the cached splits were deleted so nothing stale could survive.

New study · temperature τ

How τ trades sharpness against feasibility — F vs G, quantified

The cleanup found that G's inner optimum is exactly feasible-in-expectation while F's is not. This study measures the size of that gap and traces it through training. The first panel is the pure objective effect: for fixed random score matrices, the worst relative capacity excess maxt: μt>0 (alloct − bt)/bt of the softmax allocation at the inner optimum. The second and third panels follow the same two methods through 120 steps of real training, separating in-sample violation (μ was solved on exactly those rows — this isolates the objective's bias) from held-out violation (which adds finite-sample estimation error on top).

New study · implementation cost

Scalability in the number of treatments

The Final Report records that reviewer feedback centred on “the scalability of the implementation with respect to the number of treatments.” This measures it: seconds per outer training step as |T| grows, holding N and D fixed. It is the practical case for the Gs path — same convex objective as G, but the differentiable-convex-layer machinery replaced by a scipy solve plus a dense KKT backward.
